lesson-clerical-ability-alphabetic-filin.quote: Both records have the surname *Garcia*, so the first filing unit is tied.
lesson-clerical-ability-alphabetic-filin.note: Examples #2 and #3 now separately work the given-name and middle-name tie cases after earlier units match.

lesson-clerical-ability-alphabetic-filin.quote: Alphabetic filing puts records in letter order. The question may state the filing rule or show it through examples.
lesson-clerical-ability-alphabetic-filin.note: The opening now uses short, concrete sentences and removes the earlier abstract CSE-scope and universal-manual wording.

lesson-clerical-ability-alphabetic-filin.quote: Some surnames include words such as *De, Del, de la, van, von,* or *San*. Treat the surname the way the task tells you.
lesson-clerical-ability-alphabetic-filin.note: The special-surname passage now uses plain language and removes the difficult 'particles,' 'governing,' and 'established surname' wording.

lesson-clerical-ability-alphabetic-filin.quote: 1. The name units are identical, so move to the stated next unit, city.
lesson-clerical-ability-alphabetic-filin.note: The city tie-break case is now a worked example with numbered solution steps instead of one unnumbered solution paragraph.

lesson-clerical-ability-alphabetic-filin.quote: A **title** comes before a name, such as *Mr., Ms.,* or *Dr.* A filing system may tell you to ignore titles, or it may use them as a later filing unit.
lesson-clerical-ability-alphabetic-filin.note: The rewrite now defines a title and explains two ways a stated filing system can handle it.

reasoning-clerical-ability#1.quote: Sometimes the task shows sample names and their filed forms instead of giving the rule in words. Look for the same pattern in every sample.
reasoning-clerical-ability#1.note: The lesson now gives a local procedure for inferring a filing convention and applies it in Example #4.

reasoning-clerical-ability#5.quote: A **filing key** is the set of name parts used to sort a record. One common personal-name rule is surname first, then given name, then middle name or initial.
reasoning-clerical-ability#5.note: The rewrite explicitly identifies the personal-name components and explains their order under the stated common rule.

reasoning-clerical-ability#11.quote: If the filing rule uses the suffix as a later filing unit, compare it only after the earlier name units match.
reasoning-clerical-ability#11.note: The lesson now explains when the suffix is used and Example #6 applies it after the earlier units tie.

reasoning-clerical-ability#12.quote: A filing system may tell you to ignore titles, or it may use them as a later filing unit. Follow the rule stated in the task.
reasoning-clerical-ability#12.note: The title variant now has a local procedure, and Example #7 applies an explicit rule that titles are ignored.

lesson-clerical-ability-alphabetic-filin.quote: A filing system may tell you to ignore titles, or it may use them as a later filing unit. Follow the rule stated in the task.
lesson-clerical-ability-alphabetic-filin.note: The optional layout issue was fixed: Core Concept now flows directly into Examples, with no Speed Tricks section.

lesson-clerical-ability-alphabetic-filin.quote: A filing rule says to compare surname, then given name, then suffix. Which comes first: "Paolo Reyes Sr." or "Paolo Reyes Jr."?
